newsitem.title: USA: Clinton weighs shakeup; Christopher, Perry may go.
newsitem.headline: Clinton weighs shakeup; Christopher, Perry may go.

text.p: President Bill Clinton savored his re-election victory on Wednesday as rumblings began of a Cabinet reshuffle and White House aides pledged to try to work with Republicans to balance the federal budget.

The raucous overnight celebrations in Little Rock, capital of Clinton's home state of Arkansas, had hardly ended when U.S. officials in Washington said Secretary of State Warren Christopher was expected to resign shortly.
"I'm sure he will resign ... in the next few days," one told Reuters. But the officials said Christopher would remain in his post through Clinton's inauguration in January.
U.S. defence officials, meanwhile, said Defence Secretary William Perry had told Clinton he wants to leave the Pentagon, perhaps within a few months.

One official, who asked not to be identified, said Perry had told his staff early on Wednesday that he had informed Clinton after the president's re-election that he wanted to return to private life after three years on the job.
White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta indicated there would be staff changes and said it was hoped these would be completed by the end of the year.
Panetta, himself expected to leave, told CNN it was "no secret that at some point I'll go back to California" but that he would help get Clinton's newly reshuffled team in place.
Panetta has taken the lead on reorganizing the Cabinet while Evelyn Lieberman, one of his deputies, has been studying key White House jobs for changes.
Vernon Jordan, a longtime Washington power broker, and Erskine Bowles, a former White House deputy chief of staff, have also been tapped to lead transition efforts.

Clinton was returning to Washington on Wednesday for some more celebrating of his victory over Republican challenger Bob Dole and Reform Party candidate Ross Perot. The win was a formidable accomplishment for a man who two years ago had to insist he was still "relevant" as Republicans took control of Congress.
Panetta said the president wanted to reach out to Republicans -- who kept their majority in Congress on Tuesday -- to pass his agenda, and that balancing the budget had top priority.

"I think it is essential that we reach out in a bipartisan way, hopefully to the Republican leadership, to say, look, let us deal with the issues that the American people care about," Panetta said on NBC's "Today" show.

"I think the first priority is to sit down and work out a balanced budget, put that in place," he said. Other issues he said Clinton wanted to tackle were getting jobs for people leaving welfare, improving education and preventing crime.
Clinton will "go to the centre and try to govern for the future," Panetta said.
Officials said Clinton planned to meet with his Cabinet on Friday to discuss possible changes.

Christopher, 71, discussed his plans with Clinton on Tuesday in Little Rock. U.N. Ambassador Madeleine Albright and former Senate Majority Leader George Mitchell are considered leading candidates to succeed him. Some officials say Mitchell has an edge after helping Clinton prepare for the election debates.

Perry, 69, told his staff he had no definite date to leave and expected to stay on for at least a few months until Clinton chose a successor. Perry took the job in 1994 after the late Defence Secretary Les Aspin resigned under pressure.

There was no immediate indication of who might succeed Perry, but published reports have speculated that CIA Director John Deutch and retiring Georgia Sen. Sam Nunn are among the top candidates. Deputy Attorney General Jamie Gorelick, who previously served as the Pentagon's top lawyer, has made no secret of her desire for the job.

Apart from Christopher and Perry, questions have been raised about the future of Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary. She has been widely criticised for her official travel and her monitoring of the news media that cover her department.
Panetta told NBC on Tuesday that Republican candidates would be considered for the Democratic-led administration.
"It is going to be based, hopefully, on those who are best qualified to serve in those positions, and that could include some Republicans," he said.

Although officials insist there is no immediate deadline for Clinton to act, several have indicated he would like to announce some decisions before Tuesday, when he begins a brief vacation in Hawaii, followed by visits to the Philippines, Australia and Thailand.
